clue.text: The old man twice occupying the Northern box carriage in drag

indicators.note: twice says the word for occupying is given a second time

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father, the old man
occupying means in, as in in residence
in Yorkshire and Lancashire speech the is shortened to t'
a hearse is a carriage for a coffin, a box

explanation.surface: Dad twice moves into a Northern box and is carried away cross-dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Yorkshire speech 'the' is clipped to t', hence 'the Northern'. A box here is a coffin, and the carriage that carries one is a funeral car.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag is a tiresome nuisance, which British slang calls a pain in the backside.

clue.text: To hacks, having a hard-on amounts to exercise

explanation.surface: Journalists, ever ready, treat sexual excitement as a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: To and amounts to are joining words around the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A press-up is a gym exercise, pushing the body up from the floor with the arms.

clue.text: It's Bush's idea Zaire actually is primarily an island

indicators.note: each word gives only its primary, first letter

parts.note: the first letters of these five words spell the answer

explanation.surface: A dig at President Bush's grasp of geography, mistaking an African country for an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is a Spanish island in the Balearics, famous for its clubs.

clue.text: Not looking yourself, pissed, noticing sod all

indicators.note: drunk, so these letters are reeling about

parts.note: nothing, so the zero-shaped letter O

explanation.surface: Someone drunk, looking poorly and oblivious to everything around.
explanation.walkthrough: Not looking yourself sounds like feeling unwell; it really means wearing a disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Going incognito means concealing your identity so that you do not appear as who you are.

clue.text: Topless, passionate, flipping romantic partner gets so far

indicators.note: flipped over, so read backwards
with its top, first letter taken off

parts.note: hot, in the sense of ardent
the person you go on a date with

explanation.surface: A bare-chested, flipping eager lover gets so far and no further.
explanation.walkthrough: Flipping looks like a mild swearword before romantic partner, but it reverses the shortened hot.
explanation.definitionFit: To date is an idiom meaning until now, up to the present moment.

clue.text: Old dear's mistaken duck for Auntie's turkey

indicators.note: the letters have been got wrong, so they are rearranged

parts.note: a zero score in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: Granny has confused a duck with the BBC's Christmas turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie is the BBC's nickname; Eldorado was its notorious 1992 soap opera, axed after a year, a turkey being a flop.
explanation.definitionFit: The soap was a costly failure, and a turkey is slang for a show that flops badly.

clue.text: Give a bit of stick to Cook

definitions.text: Give a bit of stick to

definitions.meaning: to cook meat in an oven

explanation.walkthrough: Cook sits at the end like a name, Captain Cook perhaps; it is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both cooking in an oven and mocking someone mercilessly.

clue.text: Engorged with passion, getting head — a quality of the upright citizen?

definitions.text: a quality of the upright citizen?

parts.note: a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness

explanation.surface: Aroused and getting oral sex, an honest citizen's attribute.
explanation.walkthrough: Head looks like the sex act; it is the geographical word for a promontory.
explanation.definitionFit: Erectness is the state of standing straight, punning on upright as both vertical and honest.

clue.text: One-time women-only second city

parts.note: a hen party is for women only

explanation.surface: A town that was once a female-only zone, second to another.
explanation.walkthrough: One-time looks like formerly; it splits into one and time.
explanation.definitionFit: Athens is the capital city of Greece.

clue.text: Showed signs of VD: nice round succeeding point

indicators.note: succeeding means coming after, so the point leads and the remaining letters follow it
the letters V, D and those of nice are turned round into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the two letters V and D

explanation.surface: A medical case history: the patient displayed the symptoms of a venereal disease.
explanation.walkthrough: VD looks like the subject of the sentence, but its two letters are simply part of the anagram fodder with nice.
explanation.definitionFit: To evince something is to display or reveal it, so showed signs of means evinced.

clue.text: Revered personage gets to wallop court in a manner of speaking

parts.note: Diana, Princess of Wales, the much-mourned Di
wallop is British slang for beer, so ALE

explanation.surface: An exalted figure gets permission to thrash a courtier, in a figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallop looks like a verb meaning hit; here it is the old slang noun for beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is a regional variety of language, literally a particular way people speak.

clue.text: (See 14 Down)
(See 14 Down)
Problem at first getting Levis around abdominal area?

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word problem is used
the letters of Levis are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: A trouser problem: jeans that will not fit round a man's middle.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the pelvis is not strictly abdominal; it is the bony basin just below.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelvis is the lower trunk region where the jeans waistband sits, loosely the bottom of the abdomen.

clue.text: (&12/11) In the way of a willing victim of Brown's desperate measures?

definitions.text: In the way of a willing victim
definitions.meaning: meekly, as a creature led to its death without resistance
Nick Brown was Agriculture Minister in the 2001 foot-and-mouth outbreak, when flocks were culled

explanation.surface: A comment on someone going meekly to their fate under a minister's drastic policy.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2001 the foot-and-mouth epidemic led Nick Brown's ministry to order mass culls of sheep, so the idiom is literally true of the lambs.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means going meekly and unresisting to an unpleasant fate, as a lamb led to the abattoir.

clue.text: Disgustingly — yes, extremely — soused, he took out my organ

indicators.note: a disgusting state is a mess, so these letters are jumbled
only the outermost letters of yes are kept

parts.note: its outer letters, Y and S

explanation.surface: A drunk, revoltingly sozzled, boasts of having had one of the speaker's organs removed.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is Cyclops, so my organ is his single eye, which Odysseus put out with a stake in the Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer, the hero blinded the Cyclops Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant whose name this setter borrows.

clue.text: Classy, very short virgins, surprisingly enduring

indicators.note: the letters end up in a surprising new order

parts.note: V is the short form of very

explanation.surface: Posh, tiny virgins prove remarkably long-lasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Surviving and enduring both mean continuing to exist, lasting through difficulty.

clue.text: Not at a loss as regards where to prod your balls?

definitions.meaning: in snooker or pool you prod balls with a cue into a pocket

explanation.walkthrough: The second half leers at the schoolboy pastime of pocket billiards, but its fair reading is the snooker table.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in pocket means having gained money; potting a ball sends it into a pocket of the table.

clue.text: Strange, Becks' butt not likely to be featured in Hello

definitions.text: not likely to be featured in Hello
definitions.note: a plural noun phrase: people nobody has heard of

parts.note: something strange is unfamiliar, not known

indicators.note: the butt is the tail end, so only the last letter

explanation.surface: A gossip about David Beckham's backside, too odd to appear in Hello! magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine and Becks is the footballer David Beckham; the joke is that nobodies never make its pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Unknowns are obscure people without fame, exactly the people a celebrity magazine ignores.

clue.text: Peel's international body taking on outlaw Roy to a point

indicators.note: the first piece takes on the others after it

parts.note: the Scottish outlaw was Rob Roy, so the word paired with Roy

explanation.surface: Robert Peel's police force recruits a notorious Highland outlaw, up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: Peel looks like Sir Robert Peel, founder of the police; it is a verb meaning strip.
explanation.definitionFit: To unrobe is to take off clothes, and peel is slang for undressing.

clue.text: One who rubs point on Pinter's topless other half

indicators.note: the point is put on, in front of, what follows
the top, first letter of the surname is removed

parts.note: Harold Pinter's other half, his wife, was Lady Antonia Fraser

explanation.surface: Someone massages Harold Pinter's wife, who has stripped off her top.
explanation.walkthrough: Antonia Fraser, the historian, was married to the playwright Harold Pinter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber, or eraser, is something that rubs out pencil marks; here wittily cast as a person.

clue.text: Hot-headed, holding tit out, coming out with "Like some arse?"

definitions.note: an arse in British slang is a contemptible person, as is a rat, so like one is rattish

indicators.note: the word for hot-headed holds the jumbled letters inside it, like a container
out of order, so the three letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fiery woman, breasts bared, blurts out a rude question about someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Holding means the first word takes the jumbled bird inside it; arse here is the person, not the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattish means rat-like, and a rat is a despicable person, the kind British slang calls an arse.

clue.text: Like Schoenberg screwed Lana, taking time out initially

indicators.note: twisted out of shape, so rearranged
only the initial letter of out

explanation.surface: The composer Schoenberg had his way with a woman called Lana, finishing quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Schoenberg wrote music without a key centre, which is called atonal.

clue.text: Honest-to-goodness male coming beneath Brenda

definitions.note: a noun: the territory lying under the Queen's rule

explanation.surface: A genuine bloke ranks below the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so what comes beneath her is her kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom, the domain a monarch reigns over, so it lies under the Queen.

clue.text: Spotty things act out a mythical kingly character

indicators.note: the word for act is taken out

parts.note: dominos are tiles covered in spots
to do something is to act

explanation.surface: Spotted creatures perform the role of a legendary monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Act out looks like perform; it is act, taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Minos was the legendary king of Crete in Greek myth, owner of the Minotaur's labyrinth.

clue.text: Said to get a confession from a suspected flasher?

definitions.meaning: the words an interrogator says to make someone own up
read literally, an order to an indecent exposer to show himself

explanation.surface: A police officer tries to wring an admission out of a man suspected of exposing himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase urges a suspect to speak, but said to a flasher it sounds like a demand to produce the evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an impatient demand that someone tell what they are hiding, a call to confess.

clue.text: Fuss when house agent started suppressing ejaculation

indicators.note: the first letters hold the cry down between them
each word gives the letter it starts with

explanation.surface: A to-do when the estate agent began holding back his climax.
explanation.walkthrough: Ejaculation has its older sense of a sudden cry.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a commotion or noisy fuss.

clue.text: Whip on Brown, reportedly: "Drop-out"

indicators.note: the second piece follows on after the first
what we hear spoken, so a word that sounds like the one given

parts.note: Nick Brown, Labour Chief Whip and later Agriculture Minister

explanation.surface: A political whip is laid on a minister, and the gossip calls him a quitter.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Brown was the Labour Chief Whip, so Whip and Brown look like one man; Nick only sounds like the final syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: A beatnik was a 1950s bohemian who rejected conventional society, the original counterculture drop-out.

clue.text: Cook, Robin seizing Amnesty International's capital

indicators.note: the jumbled letters grab and hold the other piece inside them
to cook something is to doctor or falsify it, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: AI is the abbreviation the charity goes by

explanation.surface: Robin Cook, Foreign Secretary, seizes Amnesty International's money.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook, Robin reads as the name of the Labour Foreign Secretary listed surname first, but cook is the signal and Robin the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is the capital city of Kenya.

clue.text: Rumour-spreader needs daily scrub first

indicators.note: this piece is placed before the other

parts.note: the Daily Telegraph, a British newspaper

explanation.surface: A gossip needs a good wash with the morning paper before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: Daily looks like a cleaning lady and scrub like washing; they are a newspaper and undergrowth.
explanation.definitionFit: The bush telegraph is the informal grapevine by which gossip and news pass rapidly from person to person.
